Amla
Skin-care research: A small study of a fruit-extract toner explored facial oil control. Research on a branch-extract gel concerns a different plant part. Neither establishes oil control, hydration, wrinkle reduction or brightening from this fruit powder. Face and body packs remain possible uses to assess.

Composition and antioxidant research: Amla fruit has been studied for vitamin C and other plant compounds. Drying and processing affect composition. This jar has no verified vitamin C amount or demonstrated antioxidant skin-protection benefit in the supplied evidence.

Oral and traditional-use research: Amla has a traditional Rasayana association. Studies of swallowed preparations have explored hair, lipid and reflux outcomes; nutritional vitamin C functions also depend on verified oral intake. These findings are background about other preparations, not benefits or ingestion directions for this external-use powder.

Hair performance research: Laboratory work on extracts and hair fibres does not establish reduced breakage, softness or regrowth from the finished powder. Those outcomes require testing of the actual product.

Reetha
Body-cleansing potential: Soapnut extracts have shown foaming, wetting and detergency in laboratory studies. Body-wash use is a formulation possibility, not an established use for this jar. Appropriate skin-tolerance assessment and directions are still needed.

Household and laundry potential: The surfactant properties of soapnut preparations suggest household-washing applications. This powder has not been assessed here for stain removal, fabric compatibility or laundry performance. It is not being sold as a tested household cleaner.

Antimicrobial and mildness research: Laboratory antimicrobial findings do not make the powder a treatment for acne, fungal infection or dandruff. Foam does not establish sensitive-skin suitability, and mixed wet paste is not proven to preserve itself.

Shikakai
Body-cleanser research: A small human study examined a cleanser containing shikakai with other plant extracts. The findings cannot be assigned to shikakai alone or transferred to raw pod powder. Body cleansing remains a formulation option to assess.

Scalp research: Small studies of wash preparations and formulated shampoo have explored scalp flaking and irritation, with limited or mixed findings. They do not establish dandruff treatment from this powder.

Softness and skin-barrier claims: Softness, detangling, mildness and moisturising performance need testing of the actual product. The supplied evidence does not establish these benefits or an eczema-treatment role for this jar.

Amla
Skin-care research: A small study of a fruit-extract toner explored facial oil control. Research on a branch-extract gel concerns a different plant part. Neither establishes oil control, hydration, wrinkle reduction or brightening from this fruit powder. Face and body packs remain possible uses to assess.

Composition and antioxidant research: Amla fruit has been studied for vitamin C and other plant compounds. Drying and processing affect composition. This jar has no verified vitamin C amount or demonstrated antioxidant skin-protection benefit in the supplied evidence.

Oral and traditional-use research: Amla has a traditional Rasayana association. Studies of swallowed preparations have explored hair, lipid and reflux outcomes; nutritional vitamin C functions also depend on verified oral intake. These findings are background about other preparations, not benefits or ingestion directions for this external-use powder.

Hair performance research: Laboratory work on extracts and hair fibres does not establish reduced breakage, softness or regrowth from the finished powder. Those outcomes require testing of the actual product.

Bhringraj
Traditional skin-care association: The Ayurvedic whole-plant monograph records a traditional skin-care association known as Tvacya. This is historical context, not a human trial of a face or body pack. The supplied product information lists leaves and aerial parts, so the plant-part distinction matters.

Skin and hair laboratory research: Cell research on extracts and animal hair-growth studies use preparations different from this powder. They do not establish anti-inflammatory treatment, acne care, wound healing or human hair regrowth from this jar.

Wider traditional context: Traditional rejuvenative and liver-related uses concern medicinal contexts. They are not evidence of liver detox, sleep support or stress relief from an external-use pack. Hair softness and scalp comfort also require finished-product testing.

Hibiscus
Face and body-pack potential: Face and body packs are possible uses for assessment. Suitable product-specific tolerance and performance results were not supplied. Skin-use directions and claims about softness, shine or slip need testing of the actual powder.

Hydration and antioxidant research: Research on isolated leaf mucilage concerns a different plant part. Laboratory studies of flower extracts explore plant compounds and antioxidant activity. These do not prove hydration, wrinkle reduction or skin protection from this flower powder.

Hair-growth research: Animal and isolated-follicle studies used extracts, with different results for leaves and flowers. They do not establish human hair regrowth from this product.

Hibiscus tea is a different preparation: Blood-pressure research on Hibiscus sabdariffa calyx tea does not apply to the Hibiscus rosa-sinensis flower identity recorded for this cosmetic product. This jar is for external use, not tea or nutritional use.

Studies of swallowed preparations have explored hair, lipid and reflux outcomes; nutritional vitamin C functions also depend on verified oral intake.
